Strength-work progression schemes

Fixed-weight schemes for the heavy opening lift, where reps and sets evolve before the load moves. Lift-specific programming is in ch. 7.

PRG-43 · The "543" elevator scheme

  • Statement: For heavy deadlifts and OHP, keep the weight and build sets and reps up a ladder, then add weight and restart at the bottom.
  • Numbers: 1-3 sets of 2-5: 2; 3,2; 4,3,2; 5,4,3; then +10 lb and restart at 2. Deadlift variant 2-3-2-4-3-2-5-3-2; a tight 1, 2-1, 3-2-1 version moves slower but may allow 10 lb jumps.
  • Scope: His 2020 deadlift and OHP.
  • Confidence: medium — ~4 videos, 2020
  • Status: changed — 2020 schemes of 2-5 reps; by 2022 compounds never go below 4 (see PRG-102).
  • Sources: (My rep ranges for Natural Hypertrophy, 2020-01; How to set up evolving rep ranges (practical aspects), 2020-06; How to progress forward with evolving rep ranges, 2020-09; Weight progression on evolving rep ranges, 2020-07)

PRG-44 · Fixed-weight squat and bench ladder

  • Statement: For squat and bench, keep the weight and climb a rep ladder, then add weight and return to the start; a failed session is repeated.
  • Numbers: 4 → 5,4 → 6,5,4 → 7,5,3 → 8,6,4, then +5 lb/side; 6-5-4 (15 reps) isn't enough to jump, 8-6-4 (18) is. Higher-volume version where form breaks at high intensity: 4; 5,4; 6,5,4; 7,6,5; 8,7,6.
  • Scope: His squat and bench, 2020-21.
  • Confidence: medium — ~4 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (My rep ranges for Natural Hypertrophy, 2020-01; How to set up evolving rep ranges (practical aspects), 2020-06; When to progress forward with evolving rep ranges, 2020-08; Hypertrophy Q&A #5, 2021-01)

PRG-45 · Strength work: 1-3 sets

  • Statement: Keep strength work to 1-3 sets (4 max); 5-6 sets means sandbagging. Descending reps (5-4-3) keep the tonnage high-quality.
  • Numbers: 1-3 sets, max 4.
  • Scope: The heavy opening lift.
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (The hypertrophy series： programming strength work to bolster tonnage quality & p, 2020-11; How to use Evolving Rep Ranges for Hypertrophy, 2021-10; When to progress forward with evolving rep ranges, 2020-08)

PRG-46 · Autoregulate strength work by sets, not load

  • Statement: Keep the strength-lift weight and autoregulate through sets and reps; a weak day is made up with same-pattern back-offs.
  • Numbers: E.g. 420 lb for 1-3 sets of 4-8; a day of one set of 2 → back-offs 3-4×8-12.
  • Scope: Intermediates with a heavy opening lift.
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2020→2022
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (2 days Upper (Torso/Arm dominant) split program review, 2020-04; Why I never deload (and why you shouldn't either), 2022-02; Jeff Nippard & Alec Enkiri Want Me To Deload... I Don't Wanna (Size vs Strength , 2022-03)

PRG-47 · Top sets plus lighter volume sets

  • Statement: Pair a few top-intensity sets with lighter volume or back-off sets; how heavy the strength sets are decides the back-off reps.
  • Numbers: OHP: 2-3 top sets (or 3×2-5) + 3×5 ~20-25 lb lighter, 6 sets total (e.g. 135×5, 155×3, 145×5, 155×2); bench: top set 2-4 then 3×5; strength sets at 3s → back-offs toward 8, at 4s → heavier back-offs (5-8); deadlift 1-3/2-4 with RDL 5-7, 5-8 or 5-10.
  • Scope: Heavy compounds, mostly 2020.
  • Confidence: medium — ~6 videos, 2020
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Push Pull Legs Upper Lower 5 days split Program review, 2020-05; Coolcicada 6 Days PPL Program review, 2020-05; 4 days Upper Lower program review, 2020-06; Synchronizing evolving rep range with movement patterns, variations & rotations , 2020-12)

Rule-based alternatives he endorses

PRG-48 · The 85% rule (step loading)

  • Statement: Build reps and sets at a load until it feels like ~70% effort, then add weight to get back to ~85%, cut sets or reps, and rebuild; never keep piling volume at 70%. Your 85% grows with you.
  • Numbers: Close-grip bench 200 lb at 7/6/5 → build until the first set hits 10 and the last still gets 6 with a 4th set added → 10/9/8 at 200 → 205 lb gives ~7/6/6.
  • Scope: General, arms included.
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2022→2023
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (How to Get Bigger by Doing Less (The 85% Rule), 2022-12; How to Get Bigger by Doing Less (The 85% Rule), 2022-12; How to Get Bigger by Doing Less (The 85% Rule), 2022-12; Come with me if you want massive arms (Step by Step MASSterplan), 2023-01)

PRG-49 · Rep-goal system

  • Statement: Maxing every set at the same weight toward a total rep goal, then adding ~5 lb, is "excellent" and essentially evolving ranges by another name; he later prefers RIR for clearer brackets.
  • Numbers: 5x5 → 25-rep goal; 25 reps over 3 sets forces ~7-8 per set; when tired he'd use a 35-rep goal.
  • Scope: General.
  • Confidence: medium — ~2 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: changed — 2020: rep goals excellent; 2021: RIR preferred; 2023: day-chosen RIR autoregulation "S tier".
  • Sources: (Rep Goal System (by Steve Shaw of Massive Iron) review, 2020-07; Rep Goal System (by Steve Shaw of Massive Iron) review, 2020-07; Viking's the Bare Bones Series Program review, 2021-03; The Most IMPORTANT Methods for Muscle Growth (Hypertrophy Tier-List), 2023-11)

PRG-50 · Eastern-style big jumps

  • Statement: Keep a weight challenging for 4 reps until easy, then make a big jump; leaving reps in reserve doesn't slow progress.
  • Numbers: RIR may cost ~300 lb tonnage now but avoids plateaus and injuries.
  • Scope: General, mainly strength work.
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2020
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Why you should leave reps in the tank (Reps in Reserve), 2020-02; Why you should leave reps in the tank (Reps in Reserve), 2020-02; The hypertrophy series： applying reps in reserve while minimizing tonnage loss, 2020-11)

Static schemes (5x5, 3x5, 10x10)

See ch. 3 (INT-44, INT-45) for sandbagging and intensity.

PRG-51 · Static schemes force sandbagging

  • Statement: With static schemes the first set is too easy or the last is ground out; 5x5 progresses fast early, then plateaus hard, and is not a good hypertrophy reference.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Past the novice stage.
  • Confidence: high — ~15 videos, 2020→2025
  • Status: current

PRG-52 · Static schemes can only add weight

  • Statement: Static schemes progress only by adding weight, force conservative jumps, make tonnage jump in steps, and after a miss you deload below where you started; they never teach plateau handling ("5x5 syndrome").
  • Numbers: Repeating 5x5 needs a PR on five sets at once, which stops working after noob gains.
  • Scope: Past the novice stage.
  • Confidence: high — ~8 videos, 2020→2023
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (5 Ways to shock the muscle (GONE WRONG), 2020-07; The problem with 5x5/3x5, 2020-06; The issue with Novice Programs, 2021-03; How to Get Bigger by Doing Less (The 85% Rule), 2022-12)

PRG-53 · Where static ranges are fine

  • Statement: Static ranges are fine for novices (weight keeps rising regardless) and as deliberate tools: back-off or accessory volume after strength work, a secondary lift you don't push, chin-ups, or the only horizontal press of a low-volume day.
  • Numbers: 3x5 > 5x5 as back-off after an AMRAP top set; he uses 5×4 as a mental break on feeder lifts.
  • Scope: Novices; deliberate secondary work.
  • Confidence: high — ~10 videos, 2020→2023
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Ivysaur Novice program review, 2020-08; The hypertrophy series： understanding sandbagging to promote qualitative sets, 2020-11; Upper Body focused 5 days PPL + sprints program review, 2020-09; The Best Natural Lifter You've NEVER Heard Of (Hersovyac), 2023-04)

PRG-54 · An evolving version always beats static

  • Statement: An evolving version of a scheme always beats its static form, and static targets should not be used past the beginner phase.
  • Numbers: 3×4-6 over 3x5; 3-5 sets of 3-5 over 5x5; 3×3-5 over 3x3; 3×6 → use 6-10.
  • Scope: Past the beginner phase.
  • Confidence: high — ~10 videos, 2020→2025

Weight jumps

PRG-55 · Default jump sizes

  • Statement: The default jump is 5 lb per side on barbell lifts and 2.5 lb per side on OHP and curls, with "5 lb per hand" logic for dumbbells.
  • Numbers: 5 lb/side (10 lb total); 2.5 lb/side OHP and curls; intermediate range 2.5-10 lb/side; 5 lb/side proved too much for his curls and OHP.
  • Scope: Intermediates.
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2023

PRG-56 · No universal jump

  • Statement: Jump size depends on the lift, the range and the whole program; decide plate loading before choosing the range, and if they don't match change one.
  • Numbers: +5 lb on a 30-rep set = +150 lb tonnage.
  • Scope: Program design.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2020→2023

PRG-57 · Failed transitions mean jumps are too big

  • Statement: If you stall or transitions to a new weight fail, halve the jumps; if many transitions fail, rework the plan.
  • Numbers: 2.5-5 lb/side instead of 10; ~40% failed transitions = rework; he never failed a squat/deadlift transition but did on upper lifts until he cut jumps.

PRG-58 · Small muscles get small jumps

  • Statement: Small muscles need small jumps and microplates; 5 lb plates hurt the ego but are necessary. Don't ego lift small muscles.

  • Scope: Arms, laterals and other small muscles.
  • Confidence: medium — ~5 videos, 2020→2023
  • Status: changed — 2020: avoid microplates unless really advanced; 2021-22: ~2 lb jumps for arms and microloading for presses.
  • Sources: (Weight progression on evolving rep ranges, 2020-07; Hypertrophy Q&A #3, 2020-11; Good arm day Vs Bad arm day, 2021-01; Come with me if you want massive arms (Step by Step MASSterplan), 2023-01)

  • Status: current

PRG-60 · Coarse dumbbell jumps need a longer range

  • Statement: With coarse dumbbell jumps, extend the range so you can land at the bottom after the jump.
  • Numbers: 5 kg jumps → range to ~15, landing at 5-6.

Rate of progress and patience

PRG-62 · Slow, steady, uninterrupted progress

  • Statement: Slow, steady, uninterrupted progress beats fast gains followed by stalls, injury or regression ("not a shooting star"; the tortoise beats the hare).
  • Numbers: 3 fast months then 3 stalled months kills motivation.
  • Scope: All trainees.
  • Confidence: high — ~12 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Is the program built for small, regular increases rather than fast jumps that end in resets?

PRG-63 · Deliberately slow linear progression

  • Statement: Bodybuilders should deliberately slow linear progression to delay the big plateau, even to a crawl; there are no strength deadlines, only physique deadlines.
  • Numbers: Slow progress let his linear progression last ~6 years.
  • Scope: Bodybuilders, novice to intermediate.
  • Confidence: medium — ~5 videos, 2020→2022
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (The hypertrophy series： promoting progression in your training, 2020-06; The hypertrophy series： the perfect progression scheme for muscle growth, 2021-08; STORY TIME： My entire training history, 2021-08; Strength standards are useless, 2022-04)

PRG-64 · How fast you got strong matters

  • Statement: Slower strength gain with more accumulated volume gives more hypertrophy; how fast you got strong matters more than how strong you got.
  • Numbers: Take 70% of the gains for 10 years over 120% for two.
  • Scope: Bodybuilders.
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2021→2023
  • Status: current

PRG-65 · Gains slow but never stop

  • Statement: For a sensible lifter gains slow but never stop (a car at 1 mph still gets far); intermediate pace is the baseline, and elites progress at your rate but don't quit.
  • Numbers: Novice is ~6 months of a 15-year career; 100 → 20 mph analogy.

PRG-66 · Each lift progresses at its own rate

  • Statement: The more muscle a lift involves, the faster it progresses; OHP is the slowest after curls.
  • Numbers: +60 lb on OHP can take 2-3 years; compounds can add weight every 1-2 sessions while a curl may sit 3-4 weeks; a row can't gain 10 lb/week for a year; isolation never +50 lb/yr.

PRG-67 · Realistic post-novice rates

PRG-69 · Growth happens when progress gets hard

PRG-70 · "Natural limit" is a programming limit

Plateaus

PRG-71 · What counts as a plateau

  • Statement: Repeating a weight or reps for 2-3 sessions is the "breaking point" where gains happen, not a plateau; months at the same weight is one. Plateaus are normal and PRs every session are unrealistic (2023).
  • Numbers: 2-3 sessions = normal; ~6 months = plateau; no lift should stagnate more than ~1 month vs 4-5 months on a compound means the program is wrong (both June 2020).
  • Scope: All lifts.
  • Confidence: medium — ~5 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: contradicted — stall tolerance of ~1 month vs 4-5 months, both June 2020.
  • Sources: (The hypertrophy series： promoting progression in your training, 2020-06; How to set up evolving rep ranges (theoretical aspects), 2020-06; How to Keep Growing FOREVER (Unlimited Hypertrophy Method), 2023-07; Don't be THAT GUY in 2024, 2024-01)

PRG-72 · Plateaus are a recovery or programming problem

  • Statement: Plateaus come from poor recovery or diet, low effort, bad programming or a bad lift; in bodybuilding they usually mean too much volume to recover from or too little stimulus.
  • Numbers: Outside old age (65-70), regression means program or diet.
  • Scope: All lifters. See SLP-48.
  • Confidence: high — ~4 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (The hypertrophy series： using volume to assess recovery abilities, 2020-06; Hypertrophy Q&A #9, 2022-01; Your lifting program SUCKS! (Hypertrophy Q&A / Program review), 2024-10; So you think you can lift? (Program Review LIVE), 2024-11)

PRG-73 · First response: manipulate volume and intensity

  • Statement: Answer a plateau first with new rep ranges, more volume, widened ranges or frequency, not with new exercises; volume, intensity or supersets bypass the law of accommodation.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Stalled lifts.
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2023
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Rotating lifts： What it should & shouldn't be, 2020-05; 5 Ways to shock the muscle (GONE WRONG), 2020-07; Icecream Fitness FAQ review, 2020-06; Why spamming lateral raises won't work, 2023-12)

PRG-74 · Never deload and re-run the progression

  • Statement: Taking weight off and re-running the same progression is "a longer run-up at the same wall" and wastes quality tonnage; only drop weight if you hit failure mid-session. A missed 3x5 should become 5,4,3 instead.
  • Numbers: E.g. -10% or back to 70% resets.
  • Scope: All lifts; reset-and-retry is why many quit.
  • Confidence: high — ~8 videos, 2020→2023
  • Status: current
  • Check: Does the program handle stalls without resetting the load and re-running the same progression?
  • Sources: (The problem with 5x5/3x5, 2020-06; Hypertrophy Q&A #8, 2021-09; 5 Things I Wish I Knew Before I Started Lifting, 2022-09; The Most IMPORTANT Methods for Muscle Growth (Hypertrophy Tier-List), 2023-11)

PRG-75 · Don't swap a lift because it stalled

  • Statement: Swapping a stalled lift dodges the plateau; the "progress" on the new lift is neural relearning, and stalling is when the body must build muscle. Letting failure trigger rotation hurts mental strength.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All lifts.
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2023
  • Status: changed — 2020: never let a stall trigger rotation; 2023: only add a variation if you truly can't break the plateau; 2024: move to or add another variation of the pattern when a lift stalls.
  • Sources: (Push/Pull Pull/Legs Legs/Push 3 days program review, 2020-05; Rotating lifts： What it should & shouldn't be, 2020-05; The ULTIMATE PPL Program (Doom Slayer Physique), 2023-11; Exercise Tier Lists are STUPID, 2024-11)

PRG-76 · When truly stuck, add a same-pattern variation

  • Statement: One stimulus alone stalls; add (not swap) a carryover variation of the same pattern as back-offs or on another day. Two variations can give a year of gains before a third is needed.
  • Numbers: Incline curls stuck ~35-45 lb ×12; pull-up plateau → different grip or pulldowns; bench stalled → diversify pressing.
  • Scope: Intermediates with a long-stalled lift.
  • Confidence: medium — ~5 videos, 2021→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Pushing progression and avoiding plateaus using evolving rep ranges, 2021-04; Arnold trained like an idiot?, 2024-04; Do you look better than Silver Era lifters? (Physique Review LIVE), 2024-12; 𝐄𝐗𝐏𝐋𝐎𝐃𝐄 your Chest Gains (3 𝐊𝐈𝐋𝐋𝐄𝐑 Pec Ex, 2022-11)

PRG-77 · Plateau busters

  • Statement: For stuck lifts he endorses back-off sets, drop sets within the range, rest-pause on isolation, and occasional low-rep phases on bench.
  • Numbers: Back-off: max reps then -5-10 lb; rest-pause: 10 reps, rest 30 s, +5, then add weight; rest-pause let him add 2 lb/session instead of sitting at 50 lb.
  • Scope: Intermediates; rest-pause mainly isolation (laterals).

  • Statement: Holding strength work steady (a controlled plateau) while pushing volume or a secondary lift is a "tonnage sacrifice", not a plateau; don't try to progress a main lift and its variation at once.

PRG-81 · Fixed-increment programs rush the wall

  • Statement: Programs that add a fixed weight every session or week rush novices into the wall and then cycle deloads; "you don't force progressive overload, it happens".

Tonnage stability and strength work

PRG-82 · Tonnage rises steadily, no roller-coaster

  • Statement: Bodybuilding tonnage should rise steadily with only small planned dips, neither flat nor a roller-coaster; powerlifters wave and peak, bodybuilders don't.
  • Numbers: Never deadlift 40 lb less than last session; after each jump tonnage stays above the previous cycle's low.

Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off

He sees deloads as a powerlifting peaking tool; a bodybuilder who needs one has a program that overshoots recovery.

FAT-01 · Scheduled deloads are unnecessary for bodybuilders

  • Statement: Scheduled deloads are unnecessary or harmful for bodybuilders; needing one means you are "digging a hole" with too much frequency, volume or strength work. A deload is an emergency response to a programming mistake and useless unless injured.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Bodybuilders (not strength athletes peaking).
  • Confidence: high — ~16 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: changed — 2020: "I never deload"; 2022: he deloads constantly through set/rep management, just not the powerlifter way (see FAT-13).
  • Check: Does the program run without scheduled deload weeks?
  • Sources: (The training principles series： deloads, 2020-06; The hypertrophy series： deloading without wasting tonnage, 2020-12; Jeff Nippard & Alec Enkiri Want Me To Deload... I Don't Wanna (Size vs Strength , 2022-03; Why everyone HATES Paul Carter (liftrunbang1), 2024-02)

FAT-02 · Deloads exist for peaking

  • Statement: Deloads are for strength athletes who peak; bodybuilders never peak, so only the recovery half could matter. The term spread with the internet and powerlifting and is absent from earlier bodybuilding eras.
  • Numbers: Term spread ~20 years ago.
  • Scope: Bodybuilders.
  • Confidence: high — ~9 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (The hypertrophy series： deloading without wasting tonnage, 2020-12; Why I never deload (and why you shouldn't either), 2022-02; The Great MOGGING of Bodybuilding： How Strength Came to DOMINATE Fitness, 2022-02; Why everyone HATES Paul Carter (liftrunbang1), 2024-02)

FAT-03 · Trim the program instead of deloading

  • Statement: Reduce workload yourself before a deload would be needed; doing slightly less means you never need a week off and lose less tonnage than a deload costs.
  • Numbers: Cutting 40-50 min from your week beats a deload; ~25% more work across two weeks (2024).
  • Scope: Anyone drifting toward needing a deload.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (The hypertrophy series： deloading without wasting tonnage, 2020-12; The hypertrophy series： deloading without wasting tonnage, 2020-12; Why I never deload (and why you shouldn't either), 2022-02; Time to become indestructible (Self-Improvement Q&A), 2024-10)

FAT-04 · A week off is detraining

  • Statement: A week off, or 3-4 days fully off, is detraining, not deloading; you can only deload from a load. Time off is for injury or when away from the gym.

  • Numbers: Chest 2-3 days between sessions; biceps 3 days, so 4 sets is fine; 3rd triceps long-head session only if fresh (2023); forearm grip drill every 4-6 days (2020) vs consecutive days with different curls (2024).
  • Scope: General.
  • Confidence: medium — ~6 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: contradicted — triceps recover very fast (his own, 2020) vs slow especially if untrained (general, 2023), possibly not a real conflict; forearm frequency rose from every 4-6 days (2020) to consecutive days (2024).

The recovery pot

SLP-30 · The recovery pot model

  • Statement: Training damage drains a recovery pot whose size is your maximum recoverable volume; keep it relatively full and never empty outside a powerlifting peak. Each muscle and tendon has a pot, pots feed each other (legs also drain the lower-back pot), and time spent with the pot low wastes gains.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: General model.
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2021
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (The Recovery Pot Explained (a complete guide to muscle recuperation), 2021-02; The Recovery Pot Explained (a complete guide to muscle recuperation), 2021-02; The Recovery Pot Explained (a complete guide to muscle recuperation), 2021-02; Fullbody template review, 2021-01)

SLP-31 · Spread volume rather than empty the tank

  • Statement: Several partial drains a week give more quality work than one crash to zero; junk volume is lots of fatigue for little stimulus.
  • Numbers: Drain to 40 and refill to 100 twice (120 points) beats one 100-to-0 crash; 9 sets once a week drain to zero, 3 sets ×3/week each drain ~30% for roughly double the quality work.
  • Scope: Frequency design (see ch. 3).
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2022→2025
  • Status: current

SLP-32 · The CNS bucket holds the muscle buckets

  • Statement: The big CNS bucket spends more than any muscle but refills no faster, so leave water in the tank; it keeps refilling while you train other muscles, and its capacity is large and trainable.

5. Exercise selection & technique

This chapter covers how Natural Hypertrophy picks exercises in general (compounds vs isolation, how many lifts, rotations, order, equipment) and how he wants lifts performed (form, spine, tempo, range of motion, cheating, warm-ups) plus the technique of the main lifts, with a cue table at the end. His stance: a small, stable roster of compounds plus serious isolation, chosen to fit your build and trained for months. Every rep should be controlled, aimed at the target muscle and the same from first to last. Over time he moved toward stretch-heavy, stable lifts and strict reps. Which exercise to pick for each body part is in ch. 6; strength-specific programming of the big lifts is in ch. 7.

Compounds and isolation

Compounds give the tonnage and isolation fills what compounds miss. He counts both as required.

EXS-01 · Compounds plus isolation, neither alone

  • Statement: A hypertrophy program is compounds for most of the tonnage plus isolation for whatever the compounds miss. Compounds are the "shotgun", isolation the "sniper", and neither works alone.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All lifters training for size.
  • Confidence: high — ~25 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Does the program combine compound lifts for most of the tonnage with isolation for the muscles they miss?
  • Sources: (Isolation movements benefits： attacking muscles more precisely, 2020-03; ＂Isolation movements are useless because you can't really isolate a muscle＂, 2020-03; Biomechanics Gurus™ need to 𝚂𝙷𝚄𝚃 𝚄𝙿 about Optimal Training, 2022-10; Hypertrophy training is CANCELLED, 2024-06)

EXS-02 · Isolation is as serious as compounds

  • Statement: Isolation gets the same priority and effort as compounds, not a token "3 sets of curls" tacked on at the end where it gets skipped. It taxes the nervous system less, so be generous with it.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All; aimed at strength-template followers with small arms.
  • Confidence: high — ~8 videos, 2021→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Is isolation work programmed with real sets and effort rather than as optional leftovers?
  • Sources: (Minimalist training bad, 2021-06; We're turning Alan Thrall into a bodybuilder!, 2023-05; Is CNS fatigue out to get you?, 2022-03; The Natty FREAK with Superhero Aesthetics (Bald Omni-Man), 2023-06)

EXS-03 · Naturals skew toward compounds

  • Statement: A program that is mostly isolation is how enhanced pros train; for naturals he calls it "garbage". Naturals should lean on compounds.
  • Numbers: 70-75% isolation = the pro/enhanced pattern to avoid
  • Scope: Natural lifters.
  • Confidence: medium — 3 videos, 2021→2022
  • Status: current
  • Check: Is the program built mainly on compounds rather than ~70%+ isolation?
  • Sources: (5 Reasons why Bro Splits are Garbage, 2021-02; I was… wrong? (Giving Mike Israetel a Fair Review of RP’s Mass Gain Training, 2022-09; Will Tennyson's 4 Days Full Body Program review, 2020-12)

EXS-04 · Compound-only training leaves known gaps

  • Statement: Big-three or compound-only programs (he names BBB, Starting Strength, GreySkull) leave the long-head triceps, biceps, forearms, rear/side delts, calves, neck, abs and upper back behind. Adding rows and weighted pull-ups still misses them.

EXS-05 · The dominant muscle takes the work

  • Statement: In a compound the strongest muscle does most of the work and leverages decide activation, so some "targeted" muscles barely grow. More total load is not more load on one muscle, and the bigger a prime mover gets the more it steals from small muscles, so skipping isolation early creates deficits that are hard to fix.

How many exercises, variations and rotations

Variety should come from how a few lifts are trained, not from many lifts. Rotations swap close variations for a reason.

EXS-13 · Keep the exercise list short

  • Statement: Variety comes from what you do with a few lifts, not from many lifts. Too many exercises means each is trained too rarely, technique and tonnage become unstable, and you become "a technician of new tricks rather than a master".
  • Numbers: 20, 45 or 55 lifts named as too many
  • Scope: All.
  • Confidence: high — ~15 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Is each muscle trained with a small set of lifts done often enough to progress?
  • Sources: (The hypertrophy series： using lifting rotations to maximize quality tonnage, 2020-05; Is shocking the muscle a thing?, 2020-07; The Specificity Tree Explained (a complete guide to muscle specialization), 2021-01; Your lifting program SUCKS! (Hypertrophy Q&A / Program review), 2024-10)

EXS-14 · Exercise and variation counts by level

  • Statement: The number of exercises per muscle and variations per lift grows with training age but stays small.
  • Numbers: 2020: one method keeps a list of 15-20 lifts per body part to choose from. 2022: he rotates 6-7 favourites per muscle; biceps: beginner 1 exercise, NH 4-6. 2023: variations per lift novice 0-1, intermediate 1-2, advanced 3-5, max 5 "hard" variations per pattern. 2024: novices 1-2 exercises per muscle, never more than 4-5; small variations unlimited.
  • Scope: Novice → advanced.
  • Confidence: medium — ~6 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Does a novice program use 1-2 exercises per muscle (never more than 4-5)?
  • Sources: (4 ways to rotate lifts effectively, 2020-05; 🌌5 BIG BRAIN TRAINING TIPS TO 🆄🅽🅵🆄🅲🅺 YOUR PROGRAM🧠, 2022-05; How to Keep Growing FOREVER (Unlimited Hypertrophy Method), 2023-07; Do you look better than Silver Era lifters? (Physique Review LIVE), 2024-12)

EXS-15 · Hard vs soft variations

  • Statement: A soft variation keeps the pattern and changes the implement, grip, pause or rep range (near-full carryover, unlimited). A hard variation is a different pattern (pull-up vs pulldown, squat vs leg press), is a new skill, and should be capped. Rotate soft variations to prevent overuse without changing the pattern.
  • Numbers: max ~5 hard variations
  • Scope: All, especially intermediate+.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2023→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (How to Keep Growing FOREVER (Unlimited Hypertrophy Method), 2023-07; How to Keep Growing FOREVER (Unlimited Hypertrophy Method), 2023-07; Everything I do to get HUGE (Split, Reps, Lifts), 2023-09; Your lifting program SUCKS! (Hypertrophy Q&A / Program review), 2024-10)

EXS-16 · Change a lift only for a reason

  • Statement: Add or swap a variation only for a reason: a stall despite changing rep ranges, technique, overuse or injury. Never for boredom-driven novelty or to "shock the muscle" (he rates that D tier); constant switching keeps you relearning.

What good form is

Technique is how tonnage gets directed into the target muscle. Form rules exist, but they adapt to the individual.

TEC-01 · Bodybuilding form: target, pain-free, reproducible

  • Statement: Good bodybuilding form targets the intended muscle, is pain-free and is reproducible every rep; how much you lift is not a criterion. It may mean lifting less at first, but it recovers better and correlates with long-term progress.

Form breakdown, load and ego lifting

TEC-14 · The last rep looks like the first

  • Statement: Bodybuilders own technique from the first rep to the last: the 10th rep looks as crisp as the first, only slower. Near failure only speed changes, never form. Form breakdown is acceptable in strength sport, not for size.

  • Statement: Mechanical failure (your structure gives out before the muscle) is bad mainly because tonnage stops going to the target. You want to be limited by the muscle, never by structure. TEC-16 · Artificial vs organic mechanical failure

TEC-90 · Tight hips and squat stance test

  • Statement: Tight hips limit squat depth and make the hips shoot up on deadlifts. Test with your natural squat stance or a seated figure-four, not toe touching.

Grip and hands

TEC-91 · Straps, not mixed grip

  • Statement: Bodybuilders pull double overhand until grip fails, then strap up. Mixed grip creates imbalance and biceps-tear risk, and hook and mixed grips exist for competition (one deadlift video calls hook grip acceptable). Never mixed grip with straps or on shrugs/rows.

TEC-92 · Strap anything grip would limit

  • Statement: Use straps wherever grip would limit a non-grip exercise (rows, back work, snatch-grip shrugs, Bulgarian split squats), but not on locked pulldowns; train forearms directly. He straps rows only when needed, usually not on the first set.

TEC-93 · Stack the wrists on every press

  • Statement: Keep the wrist stacked over the forearm on any press; a bent-back wrist leads to tendinitis. Stacked wrists also make you stronger, and you shouldn't feel your wrists on OHP. Break the stack only for a clear benefit.

TEC-94 · Thumbless grip where the bar can't roll

  • Statement: A thumbless/false grip deloads the wrist where the grip doesn't need securing (curls, raises, vertical presses, reverse curls, pull-ups). Never on heavy horizontal pressing, where the bar can roll.

TEC-95 · Grip mechanics

  • Statement: A closed, thumb-wrapped grip is strongest. Set the fingers so the bar can't shift (play halves grip strength); the last three fingers do the gripping. "Squeeze the bar as hard as possible" is mostly myth.

Deadlift technique

The deadlift is a leg-driven pull with a rigid back, done positive-only. Its place in his programs is covered in ch. 7.

TEC-96 · The legs move the deadlift

  • Statement: The deadlift is "a leg press against the floor" with the back as a rigid bridge: neutral spine, very deep hips, knee flexion, strong hip drive. "Lift with your legs" is a poor cue because you always do; the problem is overusing the lower back.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All floor pulls.
  • Confidence: high — ~8 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Using the lower back as a bridge (the new lift with your legs), 2020-12; Using the lower back as a bridge (the new lift with your legs), 2020-12; Lower back rounding： The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, 2020-09; How to deadlift to maximize muscle growth and minimize injury risks, 2021-03)

TEC-97 · Deadlift setup

  • Statement: Bar over the whole foot, close to but not touching the shins. Bend the knees slightly, push the butt back and reach, then pull yourself into position so the hamstrings are tense, take the slack out, shoulders over the bar. Torso between vertical and horizontal, never parallel. Dragging the bar up the shins means you sat back too much; shoulders behind the bar means you're squatting it.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Conventional deadlift.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (How to deadlift to maximize muscle growth and minimize injury risks, 2021-03; How to deadlift to maximize muscle growth and minimize injury risks, 2021-03; Properly applying the protective and hypertrophic properties of lower body movem, 2020-10; Can lift variations/accessories affect your form on the main lifts?, 2020-03)

TEC-98 · Patient off the floor

  • Statement: Break the bar from the floor with steadily increasing leg pressure and a neutral spine, not "grip and rip". The bar leaves slowly but never slows down, and everything locks out together. People bend over to fake explosiveness off the floor.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All floor pulls.
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current

TEC-99 · The "fishing rod" deadlift

  • Statement: When the knees lock early with a rounded back, the legs leave the lift and the back finishes it, causing the struggle past the knees. Most people who fail at the knee have a setup problem, not a strength problem.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Floor pulls.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current

TEC-100 · No rounded-back deadlifting

  • Statement: No one benefits from a rounded lower back on deadlifts; it is defensible only for elite lifters or a competition PR. Olympic lifters who round do so deliberately with light, controllable weight. Abort the pull if the back rounds.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All non-elite lifters.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2020→2021

TEC-101 · Full deadlift lockout

  • Statement: Unlike other lifts, the deadlift locks out fully: hips, knees and shoulders together with a neutral spine. No leaning back, hip thrusting or hyperextension. A soft lockout usually means thoracic rounding.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Deadlift.
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current

TEC-102 · Deadlifts are positive-only

  • Statement: Don't fight the deadlift negative: put the bar down and reset. Slow negatives tire you and sandbag the positive; a controlled negative gives slightly more hypertrophy, but the concentric-only puller gets more reps and fewer injuries. Use RDLs for eccentric work; no touch-and-go.

TEC-103 · Low deadlift reps because structure fails first

  • Statement: Keep deadlift sets low-rep: at high reps thoracic extension gives out before the legs, so 15-rep deadlifts are junk volume. With shaky form, do a few sets of 4-5 and add weight only when confident. Place deadlifts early, not at the end of back day.

TEC-104 · Pick a variation that keeps the back neutral

  • Statement: If the floor is a problem, choose a stance or variation that allows a neutral back: sumo, trap bar, blocks/rack (max work off blocks, submax from the floor). No cat-back floor pulls; behind-the-back deadlifts not recommended. Deadlift range is arbitrary anyway (set by plate diameter).

TEC-105 · How deadlift variations differ

  • Statement: Variations differ in torso angle and knee and hip flexion, and torso angle plus knee flexion decide what's trained. Sumo's sticking point is off the floor, conventional's near lockout; the trap bar has more quad drive.

TEC-106 · Deadlift odds and ends

  • Statement: Learn leg drive with submaximal conventional deficit deadlifts for about 10 reps, and finish deadlift day with light hyperextensions. No heeled shoes for floor pulls (they add a deficit). If the hips shift, move one foot slightly out; a staggered stance only matters if it hurts.

TEC-107 · "Deadlift CNS fatigue" is lower-back strain

  • Statement: What people call deadlift CNS fatigue is usually lower-back strain from pulling with the back; squats are actually more taxing.

Squat technique

TEC-108 · Squat with the knees first

  • Statement: The squat is knee flexion first: break at the knees and let the hips hinge naturally at depth (limit it, don't resist it). Hinging first turns it into a good morning. Torso angle changes come from the hip, never spinal flexion, and should match on the way down and up.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All squats.
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2021

TEC-109 · The good-morning squat is the cardinal fault

  • Statement: When the hips rise first and the squat becomes a good morning, the tonnage number stays the same but the lower back takes the load instead of the quads, and it leads to injury. Fix it with technique, thoracic extension, core and glute work and 1 s paused squats, not a box.
  • Numbers: 1 s pause squats
  • Scope: All squats.
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2022

TEC-110 · Knee-dominant stance for size

  • Statement: For size keep the squat knee-dominant: medium-to-narrow stance, toes forward, knees allowed forward (knees past toes is fine); heel elevation or a slant board helps. Very wide stances raise the number but cut quad work, and a copied wide, toes-out stance repeatedly injured him.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Hypertrophy squatting.

TEC-111 · Squat depth

  • Statement: Squat as deep as you can without back or knee pain or butt wink (a "power leak"); stop before it. Parallel or a hair below is a fine heavy standard, the last few inches add little, and quarter squats stress the knees and grow nothing. Safety and repeatability beat depth.
  • Numbers: parallel or slightly below
  • Scope: All squats.
  • Confidence: high — ~10 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Hypertrophy Q&A #3, 2020-11; Injury Q&A #4, 2021-06; How to do squats for SIZE, 2022-09; Don't be THAT GUY in 2024, 2024-01)

TEC-112 · Quads are stretched below parallel

  • Statement: Quads keep stretching below parallel; the idea that quads only need a short range is a myth. Graduate to free squats once you can go below parallel, since half squats shear the knee.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All squats.
  • Confidence: low — ~2 videos, 2020
  • Status: current

TEC-113 · Controlled descent, no dive-bombing

  • Statement: Control the descent; never dive-bomb (patellar tendinitis, knees shooting forward). The bottom should feel rock solid, like sitting; reverse with a controlled bounce, practised light.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All squats.
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current

TEC-114 · Bar and upper back on the back squat

  • Statement: No pad: the bar sits tight on the skin. Use as narrow a grip as you can to pack the upper back (narrow it set by set in warm-ups), never relax thoracic extension, and drive the bar into the traps out of the hole. Grip width still depends on proportions; pad pain fades within 2 weeks to 2 months.

TEC-115 · Unrack and walk out

  • Statement: Unrack from directly under the bar with minimal knee bend and walk out in about four steps, widening into your stance.

TEC-116 · High bar vs low bar

  • Statement: Try both. Low bar suits tall, lanky lifters (bar over midfoot, back a rigid bridge); high bar suits heeled shoes and knee flexion. On low bar use a thumbless grip and press up from under the bar to spare the wrists.

TEC-117 · Box squats don't fix squats

  • Statement: On a box most people sit back, rock and good-morning up; the box catches you where the squat gets hard and reinforces forward lean. If used, go straight down and up. Touch-and-go SSB box squats are fine for glutes.

TEC-118 · No knee valgus

  • Statement: Push the knees out and press through the whole foot. Valgus may be acceptable for a one-rep max athlete but harms tendons over a bodybuilder's many reps; light paused or higher-rep squats help control it.

TEC-119 · Front squat is a rack-and-thoracic lift

  • Statement: Most front squatters (he says 80%) are limited by thoracic extension and the rack, not the legs; the lift fails when the bar dumps. Elbows high, wrists not cocked back, fingers only stop the roll (a three-finger grip is fine), torso upright. It took him about two years to learn, and he'd tell his past self not to bother.

TEC-120 · Safety squat bar folds you forward

  • Statement: The SSB pushes you forward (the opposite of a front squat), taxing the posterior chain. Never use your normal working weight the first time, and don't flip the bar.

TEC-121 · Machine squats need machine form

  • Statement: Smith machine squats are S tier with feet and hips forward, since the machine replaces the hip hinge; don't copy free-weight form on it, and novices should learn free squats. Belt squats: close stance, vertical torso, knees forward, heels elevated, not too low; wide toes-out stance is misuse.

TEC-122 · Split squats for quads vs glutes

  • Statement: For quads: front foot close, knee travelling past the toes and tracking the foot, foot straight, slow reps unless you're an athlete. For glutes: front foot further out and the torso leaning onto the thigh as you descend. Prefer split squats to lunges.

TEC-123 · Bench: shoulder safety first

  • Statement: On bench, protect the shoulders first: arch, shoulders back and tight, leg drive, elbows tucked not flared. The arch shortens the range and keeps the shoulders "in the pocket"; leg drive adds stability, not magic force. He avoids feet-up bench.

TEC-130 · Dips technique

  • Statement: Ring push-ups give a deeper, safer chest stretch than cambered bars; deficit ring push-ups are unnecessary. When spotted, tell the spotter exactly what help and how many reps you want; lift-off should be minimal and even, and you de-rack by extending the elbows.

TEC-132 · OHP: the bottom is where delts work

  • Statement: On the overhead press the bottom range (shoulders flexed under load) is where the delts work, so start low; pin presses and nose-level starts skip it (worse than skipping lockout). Elbow lockout is optional, but lock the shoulders and push the head "through the window". He never locks his elbows (tendinitis).

Pulling technique

TEC-137 · Pull with the back, arms are hooks

  • Statement: Rows and pulls are done with the back; the arms are hooks, and the back moves and stretches with the weight. Arm-only rowing is a hammer curl.

  • Scope: All pulls.

TEC-138 · Let the shoulder blades travel on rows

  • Statement: On rows let the scapulae protract so the back gets stretched; the bottom stretch matters most and pulling all the way back can be counterproductive. Constant "shoulders back" is the wrong cue for rows (pull-ups keep scapular engagement).

TEC-139 · A row is a held deadlift position

  • Statement: On bent-over rows the hamstrings, glutes and lower back hold rigid while the back pulls; floor or touch-and-go rows drift into hip hinges (his own cheat rows turned into RDLs). Novices who can't deadlift can't row safely.

TEC-140 · Barbell rows: moderate reps, pronated grip

  • Statement: Below 6 reps you jerk the bar with the legs. Barbell rows are somewhat full-body: not too strict, not too cheated. Pronated grip, no supinated or mixed grip.
  • Numbers: 3×6-10, never below 6; 5×5 "terrible"

TEC-141 · Dumbbell and Kroc rows

  • Statement: Dumbbell rows: both feet on the floor (staggered/tripod), no knee on the bench; pull in an arc so the lat stretches and the weight travels forward; no hip shifts to heave. Kroc rows: weight in front, pronated wrists, upright torso, not too few reps (5-8 invites cheating).

TEC-142 · Steer the row with elbows and torso

  • Statement: Flared elbows and a higher touch point bias upper back, traps and rear delts; tucked elbows and a lower touch bias lats (lower also rhomboids). A more horizontal torso means more lats. Never row high to the chest.

TEC-143 · Rounded-back rows, earned

  • Statement: Rounded-back T-bar rows and deep rounded rack hinges aren't really dangerous with moderate load, an engaged posterior chain and slow tempo, but they fatigue the erectors. The lumbar rule for squats and deadlifts is unchanged.

TEC-145 · Strict bodybuilding pull-ups

  • Statement: Start from the top with the negative, lower more slowly than you pull, keep the scapulae engaged, stay under the bar in line with the body, and pull with the back. No dangling or kipping, and don't force the head over the bar. Strict reps cost load but give better hypertrophy; keep the same grip and tempo when loaded.

TEC-146 · No dead hang at the bottom of a pull-up

  • Statement: A dead hang at the bottom disengages the lats and scapulae. The lat's maximum stretch is just before you lose retraction, so train that "striking range". Dead hangs are a separate tendon drill; weighted hangs don't grow lats.

TEC-147 · Pull-up grip cues and learning drills

  • Statement: Pressure on the pinkies, rotate the arms outward, elbows close, take the slack out first; use a narrower grip if wide feels all arms. Learn back-pulling with scapular engage/disengage drills on the bar.

TEC-148 · Pulldowns: vertical, slow, full stretch

TEC-149 · Pullovers: stretch the rib cage, not the shoulder

  • Statement: Lie across the bench with the hips dropped below the shoulders, slight elbow bend, elbows turned in overhead, inhale on the negative. Stretch the rib cage, not the shoulder: stop when the lat stops stretching, no full shoulder extension, and skip the dead top. If the triceps take over, bend the elbows more or use an EZ bar. Not on the floor or a bed.

TEC-150 · RDL: bent-knee, negative-first hinge

  • Statement: The RDL is a negative-first hinge with bent knees: start from a rack, push the hips back, keep the bar close (or slightly floating with the weight still under you), go until the plates nearly kiss the floor, no bounce. A stiff-leg lets the bar float away. Most people's RDLs are partials or stiff-legs.

TEC-151 · Good mornings

The lower back is a bridge, not a crane; the SSB is the best bar; use safeties, never go to failure, and treat it as the day's main hinge. 2024 hamstring version: narrow stance, feet forward, shoulders past the hips, sets of 12.

TEC-157 · Triceps extensions: only the elbow moves, no lockout

TEC-158 · Lateral and rear-delt raises

  • Statement: Laterals: slow and controlled, no swinging, stop at parallel (higher adds nothing), thumbless grip; seated or leaning versions reduce cheating. Rear delts: don't grip, hook the hand or wrist behind the handle, forearm in line with the upper arm, emphasise the bottom stretch.

6. Body-part playbook

This chapter goes through his rules one body part at a time: what each muscle needs, his rep and frequency numbers, and the exercises he prefers for it. His main point is that every muscle you want big has to be trained directly. For naturals, compounds leave the arms, forearms, abs, calves, neck, side and rear delts and the triceps long head small, while quads, glutes and hamstrings can grow mostly from compounds. His latest prescriptions (2023-2024) are more moderate than his 2020 high-volume "nucleus overload" (NO) phase: weighted, progressively overloaded isolation in roughly the 6-15 rep range.

Rules that apply to every body part

These cross-cutting rules come from the general section of his muscle-specific teaching. They apply to every section below, so they are kept here as reference rather than as numbered principles.

Chest

He treats the chest as one muscle built by a press you actually feel. Bench pressing is optional, and dips and ring push-ups do just as well.

CHE-01 · No separate upper chest; build the whole chest

  • Statement: There is no separate "upper chest" to chase; bench and dips develop it, and people who obsess over it usually have no chest. Splitting the chest into regions is an "isolationist mindset".
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All lifters; novices especially shouldn't worry about it. Multi-height cable flies are gimmicky.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (The Most Important Muscles to Look JACKED (Aesthetics Tier-List), 2024-03; 𝐄𝐗𝐏𝐋𝐎𝐃𝐄 your Chest Gains (3 𝐊𝐈𝐋𝐋𝐄𝐑 Pec Ex, 2022-11; The BEST Workout if you like to waste time for no results (Ryan Humiston Split/P, 2022-02; The PERFECT Chest Workout by Athlean-X Review, 2021-04)

CHE-02 · A stubborn chest needs a press you feel

  • Statement: Grip, arch and dominant delts or triceps can steal bench work ("225 on the bar isn't 225 on the chest"). If you don't feel a press in your chest, switch to push-ups, dumbbells or dips for a while, or superset flies or band work between bench sets.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Lifters whose chest lags despite a decent bench.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: If the chest lags, is the main press one the lifter actually feels in the chest (or has it been swapped)?
  • Sources: (Response to Husaka - CHEST - Bench vs Ring Push Ups, 2020-03; Don't turn your back on calisthenics, 2021-06; Your lifting program SUCKS! (Hypertrophy Q&A / Program review), 2024-10; Activate your chest for the bench and keep your pectoral tendons healthy in less, 2020-01)

CHE-03 · Bench press is not mandatory

  • Statement: Dips, push-ups and ring push-ups can replace the bench with no other change to the program. Choose by what agrees with you, and swap the bench if it doesn't hit your chest or keeps injuring you. His chest first grew from home push-ups, and by 2024 he had dropped the bench himself.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All lifters with a muscle goal; not powerlifters.
  • Confidence: high — ~12 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Any movement with a pain byproduct is a bad exercise (for you), 2020-02; Good chest day vs Bad chest day, 2022-05; So you think you look good? (Physique Critique Chad Edition), 2024-12; Your lifting program SUCKS! (Hypertrophy Q&A / Program review), 2024-10)

CHE-04 · Weighted dips are top tier

  • Statement: Weighted dips ("squat of the upper body") are top tier for chest, triceps and shoulders. They give more pec and shoulder stretch than bench and may stress the pecs more. The shoulder risk is slightly higher, with no safety net.
  • Numbers: He does 3 plates + 2×10 lb for 5.
  • Scope: Those whose shoulders and ribcage tolerate them; growing young men should watch for sternum or rib pain.
  • Confidence: high — ~9 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: changed — in 2020 he would not recommend dips over bench; later he ranks them equal or better for hypertrophy.
  • Sources: (Hypertrophy Q&A #2, 2020-10; The ULTIMATE Chest Exercises Tier-List (Gorilla-tier to A cup-tier), 2022-12; Response to Husaka - CHEST - Bench vs Ring Push Ups, 2020-03; Time to become indestructible (Self-Improvement Q&A), 2024-10)

CHE-05 · Ring push-ups are among the best chest builders

  • Statement: Ring push-ups, especially weighted (backpack) and decline with the rings to the armpits, free the wrists and elbows, have no floor limit, let the scapulae retract, and bias the upper chest when declined. He ranks them first in his hypertrophy tier list.
  • Numbers: About 5 sets of deep ring push-ups.
  • Scope: All levels; load them once bodyweight is easy.
  • Confidence: high — ~10 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Hypertrophy Q&A #1, 2020-09; Everything I do to get HUGE (Split, Reps, Lifts), 2023-09; Response to Husaka - CHEST - Bench vs Ring Push Ups, 2020-03; So you think you can lift? (Program Review LIVE), 2024-11)

CHE-06 · Push-ups aren't only for novices

  • Statement: Loaded, or placed at the end of a press day, push-ups stay effective for advanced lifters.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All levels.
  • Confidence: medium — ~6 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: changed — 2020: high-rep push-ups too easy for the advanced and weighted push-ups more risk than reward; 2024: he regrets dropping push-ups because "YouTube said they were for noobs".

CHE-07 · Flies and ring work add chest volume while sparing the shoulders

  • Statement: The less the shoulder is taxed, the more chest you can stimulate. Use flies, band flies and ring push-ups to grow the chest past dominant shoulders.
  • Numbers: Band flies 8-12 between bench warm-ups; cable flies 3-4x12; ~5 sets deep ring push-ups.

CHE-08 · Flies are finishers with a bent-arm stretch

  • Statement: Use flies for high reps and supersets, not heavy single sets. Top picks: low-to-high cable fly, bent-arm pec deck, fly press, barrel press, and ring flies (build up from neutral ring push-ups first). Straight-arm DB flies and the straight-arm pec deck are mediocre and risky.
  • Numbers: Low-to-high cable fly 4x15.
  • Scope: Accessory after the main press.

CHE-09 · One king press, maybe a second, maybe one isolation

  • Statement: The chest needs one big press, perhaps a second press or accessory and perhaps one isolation; more is pointless unless you specialize in chest.

CHE-10 · Rotate horizontal presses, including shoulder-friendly variations

  • Statement: Use more than one horizontal press over time, including variations that unload the shoulder: paused, close-grip, slingshot, dumbbell, football/cambered bar, pin or Spoto press. Replace one bench day per week with a paused variation.

Back, lats and traps

The upper back is where he sees the most untapped potential in naturals. A complete back needs a hinge, a vertical pull and a horizontal pull. Lats come from pull-ups and pullovers, not deadlifts, and traps come from heavy load held in the hands.

BAK-01 · The upper back has the most growth potential in naturals

  • Statement: The upper back is the most underdeveloped area in naturals and the slowest to mature; the best natural backs belong to lifters in their 30s-40s. After 10 years of training, adding upper-back volume made his grow "like weeds".
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Natural lifters, all levels.
  • Confidence: high — ~12 videos, 2020→2023
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Candito Upper Lower Hypertrophy Program review, 2020-05; My philosophy regarding upper back training (part. 2), 2020-11; Good back day Vs Bad back day, 2021-05; This is why you don't have a Demon Back (Advanced Tips), 2023-11)

BAK-02 · The upper back tolerates the most volume and frequency

  • Statement: The upper back is a "glutton for volume"; train it almost every session. Its limits are the shoulder, biceps and elbow tendons and lower-back fatigue, so favour rows and pulls that spare the lower back. 4 sets of pulldowns won't build big lats.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Intermediate and up.
  • Confidence: high — ~12 videos, 2020→2023
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (My philosophy regarding upper back training (part. 1), 2020-02; 6 days french bodybuilding split review, 2020-07; The Best/Worst of Reddit Fitness - The Ten Commandments of Lifting, 2021-10; The OPTIMAL 6D/WEEK Hypertrophy Program by Mike Israetel Review, 2022-09)

BAK-03 · Push/pull balance: from "pull more" to "many need more front"

  • Statement: He now sees many lifters as back-dominant from the "pull twice as much as you push" advice; they need less back and more front volume. Everyone should still do plenty of back work.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: Judged per physique.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: changed — 2020: do more pulling than pushing; 2024: many reviewees need more pushing.

BAK-04 · A complete back needs a hinge, a vertical pull and a horizontal pull

  • Statement: The back is several areas, each needing its own pattern; vertical and horizontal pulls are not interchangeable. Deadlifts alone give a thick "fridge" back with no width; pull-ups were the only difference between his flat and his detailed back at the same 210 lb. 6-7 back exercises is "bro-split garbage".
  • Numbers: Masterplan: 1 hinge + 1 vertical + 1 horizontal pull on different days, then +1 pull or shrug; a new hinge alternates weekly (A: deadlift 3x3, B: RDL 3x8-12); 1-2 exercises per area.

  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2024

BAK-05 · Open the back day with a heavy pull

  • Statement: Open with a floor pull/hinge, a heavy row or a weighted pull-up, never a light pulldown or machine. Don't burn out on the opener; it doubles as a warm-up.
  • Numbers: 2021: ~90% of people should open pull day with a pull from the floor.

BAK-06 · Back thickness comes from hinges as well as rows

  • Statement: The upper back works isometrically to stabilize hinge loads, so heavy hinges can replace one or two back exercises; the deadlift's weighted stretch at a 45° torso grows the mid back. Pull-ups alone leave you "flat as paper" from the side.

BAK-09 · Pull-ups are the king of lat and upper-back builders

  • Statement: Weighted pull-ups when possible; nearly every natural with big lats built them with pull-ups. They decompress the spine, barely tax the CNS, and pair well with presses and small-muscle work. Weighted beat bodyweight, which beat machines.

BAK-10 · Deadlifts and rows don't build lats; vertical pulls and pullovers do

  • Statement: At a 500-520 lb deadlift he had "essentially no lats" and wrongly blamed his insertions; the tonnage went to the rhomboids and mid traps. Slow pull-ups and pullovers then grew them. Only a few people with particular leverages grow lats from deadlifts.

BAK-11 · Do pullovers every week, short of failure

  • Statement: Pullovers transformed his lats and ribcage and are his favourite lift; put them in every program, on push or upper days. Dumbbell or machine is best; the cable version is a nightmare to set up. They supplement pull-ups and pulldowns but can't replace them.

Shoulders

Delt size comes mainly from vertical pressing. Side and rear delts are what naturals lack, so they get isolation on top, but the raises support the press and never replace it.

SHO-01 · Vertical pressing is the bread and butter of delt size

  • Statement: Most shoulder gains come from presses; the incline press is a hybrid and a delt movement first. All his recent shoulder gains came from "spamming" overhead presses. Judge by delt size, not pressing load.
  • Numbers: 70-80% of shoulder gains can come from presses.
  • Scope: All, except shoulder-dominant lifters (SHO-05).
  • Confidence: high — ~10 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Does the program include at least one vertical press a week (unless the lifter is shoulder-dominant)?
  • Sources: (Powerlifting centric Sheiko program review (part. 1, hypertrophy assessment), 2020-09; Arnold raises tutorial, 2020-09; These Lifts BUILT My Physique (Top 10 Hypertrophy List), 2023-02; Your lifting program SUCKS! (Hypertrophy Q&A / Program review), 2024-10)

SHO-02 · Lateral raises support pressing; they don't replace it

  • Statement: Big round natural shoulders come from pressing plus isolation; spamming raises at the cost of presses is a trendy mistake. Press before laterals, and never put raises right before or after a press.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: All.
  • Confidence: high — ~5 videos, 2022→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Are lateral raises added after pressing rather than replacing it?

SHO-03 · Pressing frequency

  • Statement: Vertical presses at least twice a week, building toward three; by 2024, 1-2 vertical presses plus 1-2 isolations.
  • Numbers: 2 vertical presses/week → 3 (two loaded, one bodyweight); 2021: 3-4 heavy presses/week; standing press 4x8-12 or 4x10-15; 6-10 paused; boxers 6-12.
  • Scope: Delt growth.
  • Confidence: medium — ~5 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: changed — from 2-4 presses/week (2020-2021) to 1-2 presses plus 1-2 isolations (2024).

Arms: biceps and triceps

Arms grow from isolation trained as seriously as the big lifts. For the triceps this means extensions with the shoulder flexed for the long head. Forearms have their own section.

ARM-01 · Arms need isolation; compounds alone leave them small

  • Statement: He has never seen a natural with big biceps from chin-ups alone; at the bottom of a chin-up the back takes the stretch. If rowing 3 plates didn't grow your biceps, 4 plates won't. "70% of arm gains come from compounds" is made up.
  • Numbers: He reached 16 in arms without a chin-up.
  • Scope: Natural lifters, all levels.
  • Confidence: high — ~20 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Does the program include direct biceps and triceps isolation?
  • Sources: (Response to Husaka - CHEST - Bench vs Ring Push Ups, 2020-03; The Great MOGGING of Bodybuilding： How Strength Came to DOMINATE Fitness, 2022-02; Come with me if you want massive arms (Step by Step MASSterplan), 2023-01; Why you shouldn't listen to Genetic Freaks (The Joel Williams Example), 2024-02)

Forearms and grip

Grip strength and forearm size are separate things. Forearms grow from isolation of every wrist and elbow function plus heavy weighted stretch. By 2023-2024 they were the one body part he says to "spam".

FOR-01 · Pulling doesn't build big forearms; isolate them

  • Statement: Elite 600-900 lb pullers often have thin forearms. His raw-pulling years stalled his forearms; direct work made them "blow up". His big forearms come from years of isolation, not genetics.
  • Numbers: About 13.5 → 15 in after direct flexion work.
  • Scope: All naturals.
  • Confidence: high — ~25 videos, 2020→2025
  • Status: current
  • Check: Is there direct forearm isolation, not just pulling and grip work?
  • Sources: (Having a strong grip won't give you big forearms, 2020-02; Using straps will help you grow your forearms, 2020-02; Come with me if you want big forearms (7 Steps MASSterplan), 2023-02; 10 years of lifting for this (Hypertrophy Log #10), 2025-01)

FOR-02 · Use straps; strapless pulling doesn't build forearms

  • Statement: Don't let grip limit big-muscle lifts. Going strapless or mixed-grip on back work doesn't build forearms; deadlifting for forearms is "the worst advice". Straps don't hurt forearm growth.

  • Confidence: high — ~7 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current

FOR-03 · Grip strength and forearm size are separate

Legs: quads, hamstrings and glutes

Legs are the exception to "isolate everything": they grow mostly from a heavy knee-flexion pattern plus a heavy hip hinge. Over the years he moved from back squats and deadlifts toward heel-elevated, hack and split squats and the RDL.

LEG-01 · Big legs need a heavy knee flexion plus a heavy hip hinge

  • Statement: Any squat pattern, hack, belt squat or leg press plus any heavy hinge. You can grow huge legs without squats or deadlifts specifically, but never without these patterns. The lower body needs few exercises.
  • Numbers: Squat + RDL ≈ 80-90% of the gains; a leg day = 1 big quad move, 1 posterior-chain move, 1-2 isolations.
  • Scope: All.
  • Confidence: high — ~12 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Does each week include a heavy knee-flexion (squat-pattern) lift and a heavy hip hinge?
  • Sources: (Level up your legs, 2021-06; The Smartest Push Pull Legs Routine by Jeff Nippard review, 2021-06; These Lifts BUILT My Physique (Top 10 Hypertrophy List), 2023-02; Arnold trained like an idiot?, 2024-04)

Calves and tibialis

Calves stay small because people don't train them, not because of genetics. They need load, several sessions a week, and a place early in the session or in supersets.

CLF-01 · Calves stay small because they aren't trained

  • Statement: Once trained, calves grow; small calves are bad training, not genetics. Squats don't grow calves.
  • Numbers: His calves: 16 in (2020) → 17 (2022) → ~17.8 in; an inch a year is possible. He waited nine years before training them.
  • Scope: All.
  • Confidence: high — ~12 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current

Abs, obliques and core

Abs need direct, loaded, stretched isolation. Bracing in compounds doesn't build them and diet only reveals them. He moved from daily high-rep work to weighted, progressive sets a few times a week.

ABS-01 · Abs need direct isolation

  • Statement: Compounds and bracing don't build a six-pack; bracing gives an isometric contraction with no stretch. Ab isolation is "non-negotiable", and every program of his includes at least one.
  • Numbers: ≥1 ab isolation per program.
  • Scope: All.
  • Confidence: high — ~25 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current

Neck

Everyone should train the neck directly. It grows fast on little volume. His latest prescription is 1-2 sessions a week of neck curls and extensions in the 10-20 rep range, supersetted on lower days.

NCK-01 · Everyone should train the neck directly

  • Statement: The neck ties the physique together, helps facial aesthetics, and protects you in crashes and contact sports. It grows fast on little volume, shrinks fast if you stop, and compounds stall it. A pencil neck "costs nothing" to fix; the sleep-apnea worry is a myth.
  • Numbers: His neck went from 16 to about 17 in.
  • Scope: All.
  • Confidence: high — ~15 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Is there direct neck work at least once a week?
  • Sources: (Weak point Wednesday： Neck, 2020-09; The Hardworking Lifter who BROKE the Natty Limit (Alex Leonidas), 2023-05; The Most Important Muscles to Look JACKED (Aesthetics Tier-List), 2024-03; BACK 2 THE GYM STREAM (Program reviews & Answering training questions), 2024-09)

NCK-02 · Use neck curls and extensions, not bridges

  • Statement: Bridges carry too much fatigue and injury risk (wrestlers already bridge). A harness was far better than plates or bands. Front neck: lie across a bench with a slow tempo.

7. Strength & the big lifts

This chapter covers how strength relates to size, where strength work sits in a bodybuilding program, his rep schemes for the main lifts, max testing, carryover between lifts, strength standards, powerlifting and powerbuilding, and strength for other athletes. His stance: for a bodybuilder, strength is a means, not the goal. You must get stronger to grow, but chasing 1RMs, big-three numbers or standards costs size. His own lift numbers over time are in ch. 1 and Appendix C and are not repeated here.

Strength vs size

Strength and size are linked but separate qualities. Within one person they move together, but between people leverages, skill and bodyweight blur the link.

STR-01 · Strength and size are different qualities

  • Statement: Strength and size are different qualities with some crossover, and training for one is not training for the other. Two lifters who add the same amount to a lift end up different sizes, and the one focused on volume and tonnage is bigger.
  • Numbers: example: two lifters taking a squat from 100 to 300 lb, or reaching a 250 lb bench
  • Scope: all lifters, and especially bodybuilders choosing what to train for
  • Confidence: high — ~15 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Is the program built to add muscle (volume, tonnage) rather than to raise lift numbers for their own sake?
  • Sources: (Why your strength potential might be limiting your size gains, 2020-11; The hypertrophy series： developing the values of size and strength, 2020-10; The hypertrophy series： the primordial metric for muscle growth, 2021-01; How to Get Bigger by Doing Less (The 85% Rule), 2022-12)

STR-02 · You can't grow without getting stronger

  • Statement: Strength is not the bodybuilder's goal, but you will have to get stronger to grow. Size and strength both rise, one faster than the other.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: bodybuilders at every level
  • Confidence: high — ~8 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Does the program expect loads or reps on its lifts to go up over time?
  • Sources: (The hypertrophy series： developing the values of size and strength, 2020-10; The hypertrophy series： developing the values of size and strength, 2020-10; Tips to Avoid a Mediocre Physique, 2022-11; Hypertrophy training is CANCELLED, 2024-06)

STR-03 · Within a person, strength reflects muscle

  • Statement: For one person on long-practised lifts, strength gains reflect muscle gains (bigger legs mean a bigger squat), and small size increases bring surprisingly large strength increases. Between people, leverages dominate, so you can't read strength from size.
  • Numbers: legs from 20 to 25 in means the squat went up; between people: 20 in legs squatting ~400 vs 22 in legs squatting 500
  • Scope: comparing yourself over time; not for comparing different lifters
  • Confidence: high — ~8 videos, 2020→2022
  • Status: changed — 2020: he rejected the idea that strength can rise while muscles shrink, and said size can't rise while strength stays flat; 2022: citing Candito losing size while his total rose, he said you can trade one for the other. Later view: correlated within a person, but tradeable.
  • Sources: (Response to Migan (Team3DAlpha) - PROGRESSIVE OVERLOAD IS NOT THE DRIVER OF MUSC, 2020-03; ＂What is the point of lifting natty past 30 if test levels crash?＂, 2020-04; Strength standards are useless, 2022-04; Strength standards are useless, 2022-04)

STR-04 · Strength athletes train functions, bodybuilders train muscles

  • Statement: A powerlifter squats to train his squat, and a bodybuilder squats to train quads, glutes and hamstrings. In his bucket picture, powerlifters drain the muscle buckets to fill the big nervous-system bucket, and bodybuilders do the reverse.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: choosing how to perform and judge a lift
  • Confidence: medium — ~4 videos, 2021→2022
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Minimalist training bad, 2021-06; Jeff Nippard & Alec Enkiri Want Me To Deload... I Don't Wanna (Size vs Strength , 2022-03; Is CNS fatigue out to get you?, 2022-03)

STR-05 · Specialising in one costs the other

STR-06 · Bodybuilders have "accidental strength"

STR-07 · Strong lifters need a higher threshold before size shows

Neural adaptation vs muscle

Early strength gains on a lift are mostly skill. Once the skill is learned, strength added at the same technique and bodyweight is muscle.

STR-10 · Neural gains are front-loaded and capped

  • Statement: Neural and technical gains on a new lift mostly arrive early. After that you are at 95-100% technical mastery, and further strength at the same technique is muscle. Saying all strength gains could be neural is "wrong and demoralizing".
  • Numbers: ~6 months of weekly practice (2020); "a month to a year" (2021); 95-100% technical mastery
  • Scope: any lift practised regularly, past the learning phase
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current — the window was refined from ~6 months (2020) to a month to a year (2021), with the same conclusion
  • Check: Once a lift has been practised for ~6-12 months, is further strength at the same technique and bodyweight treated as muscle gain?
  • Sources: (Strength training is for SUCKERS (Natty or not.com), 2020-07; Is shocking the muscle a thing?, 2020-07; The hypertrophy series： the optimal measure of progression for muscle growth, 2020-10; The hypertrophy series： pairing neurological adaptation and muscle gains, 2021-02)

STR-11 · Learning or rotating lifts gives artificial progress

  • Statement: Progress on a new or rotated lift is mostly relearning, not muscle. A box lets you think you are stronger at the squat. A second +100 lb on the bench brings far more muscle than the first.
  • Numbers: his SSB box squat 185→365 lb in under a year, mostly relearning
  • Scope: judging progress on new variations
  • Confidence: medium — ~4 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (Is shocking the muscle a thing?, 2020-07; Is shocking the muscle a thing?, 2020-07; The problem with 5x5/3x5, 2020-06; Why Novices shouldn't do Box Squats, 2021-01)

STR-12 · Strength is largely skill

  • Statement: Strength is largely the skill of recruiting motor units in a pattern, and it needs a fresh nervous system. High-frequency programs (daily squatting, Bulgarian or Wisconsin-style) raise one lift without much muscle, and he never prescribes them for size.

  • Scope: specialised strength programs
  • Confidence: medium — ~6 videos, 2020→2022

STR-13 · Big strength jumps without visible change are a red flag

  • Statement: Past the novice stage, a big percentage strength gain with no muscle gain is biologically impossible. Strength that jumps while nothing visibly changes is a red flag.
  • Numbers: +100 lb on chin-ups, dips and OHP should visibly change you
  • Scope: past novice; judging your own or others' claims

  • Statement: Time off costs strength and work capacity well before it costs size. Presses, especially the OHP, regress quickly when not practised.

  • Scope: breaks and returns to training

Bodyweight, fat and leverage

Bodyweight makes you stronger, but strength that comes from fat is leverage, not progress.

STR-15 · Fat-driven strength isn't real progress

  • Statement: Mass moves mass, but strength gained by adding mostly fat raises absolute strength, not pound-for-pound strength. It is leverage, and it disappears on a cut.
  • Numbers: +20 lb on the bench with +20 lb bodyweight = no real progress; +100 lb of mostly fat raises absolute strength only
  • Scope: judging progress during bulks
  • Confidence: high — ~6 videos, 2020→2022
  • Status: current
  • Check: Is strength progress judged at a stable bodyweight (or alongside lean gain), not credited when it only follows fat gain?
  • Sources: (Response to Migan (Team3DAlpha) - PROGRESSIVE OVERLOAD IS NOT THE DRIVER OF MUSC, 2020-03; BLOATMAXX： the Kyriakos Grizzly example, mogging general & potential downsides, 2020-12; Don't fall for the bulking meme, 2022-11; Don't fall for the bulking meme, 2022-11)

STR-16 · Bodyweight helps presses far more than hinges

  • Statement: Extra bodyweight helps pressing through leverage (a shorter range of motion) and helps hinges much less. In a deficit, hinges barely suffer while bench and OHP drop a lot.
  • Numbers: "put 50 lb on your frame, add ~100 lb to your bench"; he benched 315 at ~220 lb, 335 when fatter, and lost it when the fat came off
  • Scope: pressing vs hinging lifts across bulks and cuts
  • Confidence: medium — ~5 videos, 2020→2021
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (BLOATMAXX： the Kyriakos Grizzly example, mogging general & potential downsides, 2020-12; Crazy bulks： secret for INSANE gains?, 2021-11; Crazy bulks： secret for INSANE gains?, 2021-11; The reason people lose so much strength/size on cuts, 2020-09)

STR-17 · Pure strength needs mass, preferably muscle

  • Statement: For pure strength, carry as much mass as possible, preferably muscle. Getting really strong means letting bodyweight rise, so staying very lean ("otter mode") means never getting really strong or reaching full size.

  • Scope: lifters whose goal is maximal strength

Strength work inside a bodybuilding program

Strength work is a small, focused part of a bodybuilding program. It opens the session, is done as solo sets, and serves the tonnage. His later practice moved the heavy work to less risky movements.

STR-21 · Strength work is a year-round pillar

  • Statement: A small dose of heavy strength work is the backbone of hypertrophy training and stays in all year, not only in a block. It is little tonnage, but its high-intensity peaks drive progression.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: all bodybuilding programs
  • Confidence: medium — ~10 videos, 2020→2021 (strongly stated early, less emphasised later)
  • Status: changed — 2020-21: the backbone, "the one cornerstone you never cut"; 2024-25: high-bar squat and bench only 3-5 times a year, he "doesn't care about strength", and his heavy work moved to dips and weighted pull-ups. Later view: keep getting stronger, through less risky movements.
  • Check: Does the program keep some heavy, low-rep work all year rather than only in phases?
  • Sources: (How to progress forward with evolving rep ranges, 2020-09; The hypertrophy series： utilizing tonnage for muscle growth, 2021-01; You know what time it is... STORY TIME, 2025-01; 3 hours of Story Time, 2025-02)

STR-22 · Strength work opens the session

  • Statement: Strength work comes first, and a day with zero strength work is bad, with occasional exceptions. Pre-activation must be light: an explosive opener taken short of failure (a kettlebell swing) primes you, while a leg-curl opener only fatigues. A small dose fires up the nervous system for the accessories.

Rep schemes for the main lifts

His rep ranges for the main strength lifts. A summary table follows the principles.

STR-34 · Deadlift: few sets, never more than 5 reps

  • Statement: Deadlift for 1-3 sets of 2-5 reps, never more than 5, and a single heavy set of 5 is often enough. 3x3 works very well if you leave reps in the tank.
  • Numbers: 1-3 x 2-5; often 1x5; 3x3 with reps in reserve; 3x5 is a good volume for floor pulls; back-offs 4x3 at a comfortable triple or 3x3 submax
  • Scope: heavy floor pulls, intermediate and up
  • Confidence: high — ~14 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current

STR-35 · Novice deadlift: sets of 6, no high-rep maxes

Max testing

Bodybuilders build strength and estimate it from reps. They don't test it.

STR-44 · Never test 1RMs as a bodybuilder

  • Statement: Maxing out is a powerlifting skill for peaking and brings no hypertrophy benefit. 1RMs don't even build strength (2-3RMs or 1 rep in reserve might), and every max-out uses up muscle-building capacity.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: bodybuilders
  • Confidence: high — ~7 videos, 2020→2024
  • Status: current
  • Check: Does the program avoid 1RM testing?
  • Sources: (AlphaDestiny Novice Program review (part. 2： FAQ), 2020-04; 5 reasons to only lift heavy weight DEBUNKED, 2021-01; No one understands training intensity, 2021-11; Powerbuilding is an Abomination., 2023-10)

STR-45 · Estimate your max from reps

  • Statement: Estimate your max from rep performance and program by intensity. A double just under your max beats a single: double the tonnage, with less risk and fatigue.
  • Numbers: e.g. 200x10; 485x2 vs 500x1; by 2021 he hadn't tested a 1RM in ~4 years
  • Scope: bodybuilders
  • Confidence: medium — 1 video, 2021
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (No one understands training intensity, 2021-11; No one understands training intensity, 2021-11; No one understands training intensity, 2021-11)

STR-46 · Constant max testing stalls progress

  • Statement: Testing your max often "smashes the piggy bank": it spends what you have built instead of building more.
  • Numbers: testing a deadlift 1RM every 2 weeks kept him at 465-485 lb for a year
  • Scope: anyone who tests maxes frequently
  • Confidence: medium — 1 video, 2024
  • Status: current
  • Sources: (The WORST Bodybuilding Program Ever Created (my bad), 2024-04)

Carryover between lifts

The best way to improve a lift is to do that lift. Variations help, but partials, machines and odd lifts can hide your real strength.

STR-47 · Specificity wins

  • Statement: The best way to bench more is to bench, and the best deadlift accessory is more deadlifting.
  • Numbers: —
  • Scope: improving a specific lift
  • Confidence: medium — ~3 videos, 2020→2024
